title: The Soviet five-day week
hook: For about a decade the Soviet Union lived without a seven-day week.
peek: In 1929 the Soviet Union replaced the seven-day week with a five-day cycle. Workers were split into colour-coded groups with staggered days off, so factories never stopped. Families often found they no longer had a day off together.
lede: In the autumn of 1929 the Soviet Union introduced the nepreryvka, or continuous working week. The week shrank to five days, and the common day of rest disappeared. Each worker was put into one of five groups, each with its own colour and its own rest day, so that on any given day a fifth of the workforce was off and the factories never closed.

bullets.text: Each of the five groups had a colour, and calendars of the time showed every day marked with the colour of the group that had it off.

The flaw was social. A husband and wife could be assigned different colours, so their days off never lined up. Many people complained that they rarely saw relatives or friends, and some factories struggled with machines running nonstop.
From 1931 most workers moved to a six-day week with a shared rest day on the 6th, 12th, 18th, 24th and 30th of each month. Official calendars numbered the days instead of naming them.
In June 1940 the Soviet Union went back to the ordinary seven-day week with Sunday as the common day off, ending the experiment after about a decade.
